subject: research/interval-elicitation
professional: a mechanism-design / forecast-evaluation statistician who has refereed work on proper scoring rules and elicitability (Gneiting-Raftery, Lambert-Pennock-Shoham, Frongillo school). They would check first that the regret formulas are right for non-symmetric and heavy-tailed laws, that the shortest-interval claim is not just the textbook HPD, that the sample-size comparison uses a fair baseline, and what is new against the elicitability literature.

evidence.correctness: Ran `cd research/interval-elicitation && PYTHONPATH=src python3 experiments/run.py > out.txt; diff out.txt experiments/results.txt`: identical (0.8 s, pure stdlib, deterministic). Then wrote scratchpad indep.py using scipy 1.17.1 / numpy 2.4.6 and NOT importing the package (scipy.stats pdf/cdf/ppf, scipy.integrate.quad on the expected score, scipy.optimize for the shortest interval, 20M-draw Monte Carlo for detection). Recomputed: (1) E1 normal interval-score regret, alpha=0.05: lam=0.9 gives 0.10214 (reported 0.1021), lam=0.5 gives 4.2076 (4.2076); alpha=0.32 lam=2 gives 1.04576 (1.0458). (2) E2 Cauchy alpha=0.1, finite regret by quad of the score difference against the Cauchy density: halving 2.35766 (2.3577), doubling 3.84171 (3.8416). (3) E3 lognormal(0,1) shortest interval via minimising u-l subject to F(u)-F(l)=c: 80% coverage width 2.2805, 31.4% shorter, lam=1/f(l)=1/f(u)=8.408 (reported 2.281, 31%, 8.41); 95% coverage [0.02609, 5.1869], width 5.1609, 25.8% shorter, lam 50.40 (reported 5.161, 26%, 50.40, lower end 0.026 vs 0.141). (4) E4 detection n by Monte Carlo of the paired payment difference: alpha=0.5 IS 325.3 / H 15898 (reported 324.0 / 15730), alpha=0.1 IS 175.6 / H 526.2 (174.6 / 525.3), alpha=0.01 IS 321.1 / H 370.5 (319.8 / 369.7): agree within Monte Carlo error (~0.5 to 1%). The ratios behind the lede ('3 to 48x', '1.2x at alpha=0.01') recompute as 3.0, 48.9 and 1.15. I did not independently check E5 curvature beyond reading that its theory columns (2/alpha f(z), z) follow from the second derivative. All checked numbers right.
evidence.completeness: Checked each claimed item. README: 'stdlib-only' true (model.py imports only math); '9 tests, <2 s' true (`PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`: Ran 9 tests in 0.471s, OK); `experiments/run.py` reproduces results.txt byte for byte; `python3 experiments/figure.py` ran and rewrote detection.svg with no git diff; live page https://marisstella.app/research/interval-elicitation/ returned HTTP 200 (I did not read its content). Paper: Winkler regret formula, Cauchy finite regret, scale-misreport closed form, level-set optimum, bounded payment, symmetric equivalence, E1-E5 tables all exist in code and results.txt; the paper tables match results.txt line by line. No TODO or stub found. Gaps against the title's promise: it is a purely analytic study of known distributions (normal, lognormal, Cauchy); nothing is estimated from data, and the paper itself says no estimation-error rate is proved.
evidence.verification: Test command: `PYTHONPATH=src python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -v`, 9 tests, OK. The tests are reasonable (closed-form comparison, a 400k-draw Monte Carlo, level-set first-order check, local optimality of the HPD interval). Seeded mutations in src/interval_elicitation/model.py, each applied by exact-string replace with a git diff check and reverted by git checkout (tree clean afterwards): (1) pinball_regret for the upper endpoint uses tau=alpha/2 instead of 1-alpha/2: CAUGHT (3 failures). (2) hpd_diff_moments mean sign `p1_only - p2_only` -> `p2_only - p1_only`: CAUGHT (1 failure). (3) hpd_diff_moments second moment `p2_only*(dw-lam)**2` -> `(dw+lam)**2` (wrong variance, drives the headline detection counts): NOT caught, 9 OK; the variance test compares a ratio with places=1, i.e. tolerance 0.05. (4) detection_n `var/(mean*mean)` -> `var/abs(mean)`: NOT caught, 9 OK; detection_n and the whole E4 table (the source of the 3-48x claim) have no test at all. (5) _mode lognormal `exp(m - s*s)` -> `exp(m - s)`: NOT caught, but this only seeds a bracketing start for the search and is near-equivalent for s=1. (6) `pdf(x0) <= c` -> `<`: NOT caught; boundary case, near-equivalent. So of 4 non-equivalent mutations 2 were caught, and the two that survived sit under the paper's central quantitative claim. diff_moments (quadrature, used for the S column of E4) is only tested indirectly, and the test of its Monte Carlo twin is loose.
evidence.craft: Read model.py (185 lines), run.py, test_model.py, figure.py header, pyproject.toml. Readable, documented in the module docstring, stdlib-only, small. Defects: (1) no input validation anywhere: alpha outside (0,1), l>u, lam<=0 give ZeroDivisionError, silent nonsense, or a negative-width 'interval' (e.g. hpd_interval(0, d) divides by zero; quantile(t) with t outside (0,1) loops until 200 bisections return a bracket end). (2) diff_moments takes hard-coded integration limits (run.py passes -14, 14) so a lognormal or Cauchy caller silently truncates the tails; the kink points of the score (l, u) are not placed on the Simpson grid, so accuracy rests on n=60000 (it matches Monte Carlo to ~0.5% here). (3) Tuples ('normal', loc, scale) with an `else` branch for lognormal: an unknown kind string silently becomes lognormal (cdf/pdf/quantile fall through). (4) hpd_level is exported and unused; expected_is_normal has a `* -1` idiom and an mu/s parameter pair used nowhere else. (5) results are printed, not asserted, so run.py cannot fail. (6) `from .model import *` plus a long __all__ is a flat namespace of 24 names. (7) pure-Python quadrature makes quantile-in-a-loop slow; fine at this size. No copied engines, no network, no silent fallback beyond (3).
evidence.claims: Checked each README/paper claim against a file. Backed: Winkler regret formula (test_regret_vs_closed_form_normal, test_regret_vs_simulation, E1-E2); finite Cauchy regret (test_cauchy_regret_finite_and_positive, E2); H bounded in [0, width+lam] (test_bounded_payment); level set f(l)=f(u)=1/lam (test_hpd_is_level_set_and_optimal); '22 to 31 percent narrower' and the E3 table (results.txt and my recompute); '3 to 48x larger detection sample for alpha >= 0.1' (E4: 525/175=3.0 to 15730/324=48.5) and '1.2x at alpha=0.01' (370/320); curvature k values (E5); '2 to 3x at 90 to 95 percent' (525/175, 381/192). Limits section is real: risk-neutral verifiers, unimodal, one report, one lognormal shape, no estimation-error rate. Weaknesses, none a wrong number: (1) the paper's 'property-elicitation view (Frongillo and coauthors)' and Winkler's score carry no citations; there is no reference list at all. (2) The README and paper give no AI-produced note or not-advice line (research, so not required by the product rules, but other research READMEs carry one). (3) 'the shortest interval for its coverage' is exact only for unimodal laws; stated in Limits, not in the lede. (4) The 3-48x figure is presented as 'what boundedness costs' but is for one alternative (a 20 percent symmetric shrink of a normal), see domain.
evidence.fitness: Research bar (research/CLAUDE.md: PhD-level programme, publishable, deep-tech application). A researcher can reuse the exact-regret code and the E4 detection machinery, and the Cauchy/finite-regret and curvature (2/alpha f(z)) results are clean. But the project is a single 185-line analytic note on three textbook distributions, one author-chosen alternative, no data, no estimation, no theorem beyond first-order conditions, and it is not an entry in research/PROGRAMMES.md (grep found none). I would not call it a programme-grade result or a paper a main-track venue would take as is; it is a sound technical note. Nearest prior work: Winkler 1972 and Gneiting and Raftery 2007 (interval score is proper and equals two pinball losses; regret as a Bregman-type integral); Gneiting 2011 on quantiles and elicitability; Lambert, Pennock and Shoham 2008 and Frongillo and Kash on elicitation; Heinrich 2014 (the mode is not elicitable) and Dearborn and Frongillo on the modal interval / indirect elicitability of the mode; the textbook fact that the HPD region is the shortest region of given coverage. I could not fetch these offline and cite them from memory, so treat the attributions as to-be-verified. Judgement: the formulas are sound; equal-tailed vs HPD and score-vs-0/1-style losses are known ideas, the exact Cauchy regret and the detection-sample cost comparison are the closest thing to new, and the latter rests on an unfair baseline (see domain). Sound, modestly new at best.
evidence.domain: Compared with proper-scoring-rule and elicitation practice. Matches: Winkler score as sum of two pinball losses, regret as an integral of F minus tau between the true and reported quantile (finite without a mean, a nice point), and the HPD characterisation. Departs or is missing: (1) the fairness of the E4 comparison: the paper attributes the 3-48x cost to bounded payment, but H differs from S in two ways at once (bounded and shortest-interval). The natural bounded competitor, the interval score with the miss penalty clipped (or a truncated pinball loss), is not computed, so 'what boundedness costs' is not isolated; H is also a coverage-indicator loss, whose information content is known to be poor, which the 3-48x number largely reflects. (2) The question a deployed verifier faces is estimating the interval from samples; no estimation error, finite-sample bias or incentive-to-misreport under noisy outcomes is studied (the paper says so). (3) lam must be set from the coverage you want and the unknown law: the paper notes lam=385 for 99 percent on lognormal, but there is no discussion of how a market maker would choose lam without knowing F, which is the practical obstacle. (4) The detection test is a one-sided z=1.645 normal approximation of a paired mean difference; for H at small n the payoff is a three-point distribution and the normal approximation is poor, so the n values are asymptotic. (5) The 'strictly proper' wording needs F strictly increasing, which is stated for S but H's uniqueness for non-unimodal F is only noted in Limits. A referee would accept the exact-regret part and ask for the clipped-S baseline, a reference list, and an estimation study.

defects.what: Seeded mutations in the variance of the paired-difference payoff (hpd_diff_moments second moment) and in detection_n both leave all 9 tests passing; the E4 detection table, the source of the headline '3 to 48x' claim, has no direct test, and the only variance test uses places=1 on a ratio.

The sample-size comparison conflates boundedness with the shortest-interval/coverage-indicator design; no clipped interval score baseline is computed, so the paper's 'what boundedness costs in samples' is not isolated by the experiment.
No references: the property-elicitation framing, the Winkler score, the HPD and the mode/modal-interval elicitability literature are uncited, so novelty cannot be judged from the paper.

No input validation (alpha outside (0,1), lam<=0, l>u raise ZeroDivisionError or return nonsense); an unknown distribution kind silently falls through to lognormal; diff_moments integration limits are caller-supplied and silently truncate heavy tails.
run.py only prints; nothing asserts its results, and dead code remains (hpd_level unused, expected_is_normal `* -1` idiom).

verdict: A small, correct analytic note. I recomputed the interval-score regrets (normal and Cauchy), the lognormal shortest-vs-equal-tailed widths and multipliers, and the E4 detection sample sizes with an independent scipy/Monte Carlo implementation and every number matched, and the committed results.txt and figure reproduce exactly; the README and paper claims are backed by files and carry honest limits. It does not meet the bar: verification is 2 because mutations in the variance and in detection_n, which underpin the headline '3 to 48x larger sample' result, are not caught (2 of 4 non-equivalent seeded mutations survived), and the median of the seven scores is 2 because the project is thin as research: a single hand-chosen alternative, three textbook distributions, no estimation or data, no reference list, an unfair baseline for the boundedness claim (no clipped interval score), and prior work (Winkler, Gneiting-Raftery, HPD, mode elicitability) that covers most of the ideas. It is finished for its stated scope and sound, but not new enough or deep enough to be called a programme result. Fixes are small: test detection_n and the variance tightly, add a clipped-S baseline, add references and input validation.
